stories.headline: Nepal flash floods highlight need for planned settlement, scientific assessments: Experts
stories.title: Nepal flash floods highlight need for planned settlement, scientific assessments: Experts
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 30: The devastating flash floods in Nepal have driven home important lessons of undertaking systematic scientific assessments of glaciers in order to understand and mitigate hazards and to develop a land use policy in the Himalayan region, experts said. Over 460 people from Nepal and Tibet have been killed, and thousands, including Indian tourists, are missing after massive flash floods hit parts of Nepal on Wednesday, wreaking havoc across several towns and villages, washing away critical bridges and crippling a dozen hydropower projects. Initial speculation after a sudden surge near the Nepal-Tibet border crossing in Rasuwagadhi included a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) and an avalanche. However, researchers from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), based near Kathmandu, are investigating whether an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-altitude location may have triggered the floods. A large volume of ice and rock debris may have entered the Lende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi River, which could have generated a sudden surge carrying water, sediment and large boulders downstream, they said, based on a preliminary assessment of video footage and information from affected areas. "It is related to climate change because the snow covers are reducing, the glaciers are receding, more rocky or barren areas are exposed -- they absorb more heat, which makes the slopes more vulnerable," Mohd Farooq Azam, senior cryosphere specialist at ICIMOD and associate professor at the Indian Institute of Technology Indore, told PTI. Even though the exact cause is yet to be ascertained, he added, it may be a result of less snow cover, receding glaciers, and some permafrost degradation in the area. Extreme precipitation events, especially heavy snowfall, in the Himalayas only temporarily increase snow accumulation, a study published in Global and Planetary Change has found. Climate change has also contributed to an increase in glacial lakes in Himachal Pradesh, with a recent study, published in the Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, showing an increase of 525 per cent in the lakes between 1990 and 2024, with a doubling in area. Smaller lakes have increased from nine in number to 487. "There are different mechanisms through which glacial lakes can form. They may be dammed by moraines, glacier ice, bedrock depressions, or other geomorphological features," author Reet Kamal Tiwari, associate professor and head, department of civil engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Ropar, Punjab, told PTI. However, the mere presence of a glacial lake does not necessarily mean that it poses an immediate threat to nearby communities, he said. "We first need to assess the vulnerability and stability of the lake and identify the possible external triggers that could lead to a sudden release of water. The concern is not simply the increasing number of glacial lakes; it is the combination of increasing hazard potential and increasing downstream exposure," Tiwari said. Triggers may include landslides, intense rainfall, snow or ice avalanches, rockfalls, or the collapse of a hanging glacier, he said. Soniya Rijal, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Sydney in Australia, said that a lack of a warning system built only around rain-related events also contributed to the disaster. "What this event shows is that our warning systems, formal and informal, are built around rain. I have heard that people in the affected valleys were alerting their neighbours before the water arrived, but because there had been no heavy rainfall, many did not take the warnings seriously," she said. Rijal is from Kathmandu. Azam said, "We have very limited data. We need to improve data, the basic understanding on the ground, and develop specific models for the Himalayan region and early warning systems, especially low-cost ones, so that we can install it many places wherever we have hot spots." The flash floods are similar to those in Chamoli, Uttarakhand, when a massive ice and rock avalanche from the Ronti peak triggered a sudden surge of water, impacting the Rishi Ganga, Dhauliganga, and Alaknanda rivers in February 2021. Hydropower projects were severely damaged and about 300 people, mostly workers at the dam sites, were reported killed or missing. "Every disaster is unique. First, we need to understand the processes, and then we need to design some mitigation measures accordingly," Azam said. Tiwari said, "The first requirement is proper scientific assessment of potentially hazardous glacial lakes and their downstream areas." "A proper assessment should examine the lake, its dam and surrounding terrain, possible triggering mechanisms, downstream flow paths, and the settlements and infrastructure that could be affected," he said. Authorities should involve experts with appropriate experience in glaciology, geomorphology, hydrology, remote sensing, geotechnical engineering, and disaster management, Tiwari added. Further, the flash floods drive the urgency of developing land use policies, Azam said. "The problem is we are settling very close to the river and sometimes on the river. The urgency is to develop a land use policy," he said. "There should be proper planning for the settlement infrastructure development, because these events will happen and we understand that over the last couple of decades, the frequency as well as magnitude of such events have increased," he added. Azam also pointed to how there needs to be an assessment of how the environment can impact infrastructure. "When we develop an infrastructure, we have to do environment impact assessment. But now is the time when we need to do environment's impact assessment on the infrastructure," he said. "If there is some heavy rainfall, some cloud burst, some glacial lake outburst flood, or something like what happened yesterday, what would be the impact on the settlement and infrastructure? So we don't have this kind of assessment anywhere," Azam said.

stories.headline: India steps up rescue efforts in flood-hit Nepal as 275 Indians remain missing
stories.title: India steps up rescue efforts in flood-hit Nepal as 275 Indians remain missing
stories.summary: India steps up rescue efforts in flood-hit Nepal as 275 Indians remain missing
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: More than 275 Indians remain missing after flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, the government said.
India has stepped up rescue efforts, sending fresh teams, relief supplies and forensic support as search and recovery operations continue.
More than 275 Indians remained missing and 108 others had been rescued after the flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border four days ago, the Ministry of External Affairs said on Saturday.
The ministry also said 128 persons of Indian origin remained uncontactable.
The MEA said 598 Indian nationals had safely crossed into Nepal from China in the last two days, while around 900 Indians were still on the Chinese side but were "safe and contactable".
It also said India had sent fresh relief material and technical teams to support rescue and recovery efforts in Nepal.
In a statement, the MEA said, "Till date, 108 Indian nationals have been rescued in Nepal, and contact was re-established with around 50 Indian nationals who were earlier uncontactable.
Furthermore, 598 Indian nationals have safely crossed into Nepal from China in the last two days, as per local government sources in China."
"Around 900 Indian nationals are still on the Chinese side but are safe and contactable.
Unfortunately, more than 275 Indian nationals and 128 persons of Indian origin remain missing or non-contactable," it said.

The ministry said four Indian nationals – Ripu Kumar, Chaneshwar Narzary, Kripa Shankar and Mohammed Minhajuddin – were rescued from a hydropower project in Rasuwa and were expected to reach Kathmandu soon.
Rasuwa was among the areas severely hit by the floods.

stories.headline: It's Deeply Disappointing
stories.title: It's Deeply Disappointing
stories.summary: The decision to increase electricity tariffs in Jammu & Kashmir at a time when ordinary families are already struggling with the rising cost of living is deeply disappointing. More importantly, it raises a fundamental question of political accountability: what happened to the promises made to the people before the Assembly elections? The Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission has approved an average tariff increase of 6.83 per cent, applicable from September 1, 2026. For metered domestic consumers, the rate for consumption up to 200 units has increased from ₹2.30 to ₹2.45 per unit; for 201–400 units, from ₹4.00 to ₹4.20; and above 400 units, from ₹4.35 to ₹4.60 per unit. These figures may appear small when viewed from the comfort of government offices. For an ordinary household, however, every additional financial burden matters. From promise of relief to reality of higher bills The National Conference went before the electorate promising 200 units of free electricity. That promise naturally created expectations among families that desperately needed relief. Today, instead of experiencing the promised relief, consumers are confronting increased tariffs. The government may argue that its promise of free electricity and the general electricity tariff are technically separate matters. But politics cannot be reduced to technical explanations. The real question is what an ordinary voter understood when promises of cheaper or free electricity were made. People vote on the basis of promises and the reasonable expectations created by those promises. If financial constraints, distribution losses and the cost of purchasing electricity were realities after the election, they were realities before the election as well. Governments cannot discover economic realities only after obtaining the mandate of the people. Kashmir's winter cannot be viewed through ordinary consumption calculations The impact of electricity prices assumes an even greater significance in the Kashmir Valley. For people sitting outside Kashmir, electricity may be regarded primarily as a source of lighting and running household appliances. During Kashmir's severe winter, electricity is intimately connected with survival, warmth and basic human comfort. Temperatures fall below freezing in many areas. Water pipes freeze. Snowfall disrupts normal life. Families depend increasingly upon electric heaters, boilers, geysers, heating blankets and other appliances. The elderly, children and economically weaker families suffer the most. This means that electricity consumption during the harsh winter months cannot simply be treated as discretionary consumption. A Kashmiri family using additional electricity to keep its children or elderly parents warm is not indulging in luxury. It is responding to climatic necessity. And the timing is particularly unfortunate. The revised tariff becomes applicable from September 1 and will remain applicable through the approaching winter until March 31, 2027. The government should therefore ask itself a simple question: Is the period immediately preceding the harsh Kashmir winter the appropriate time to make electricity more expensive for households? Don't make consumers pay for inefficiency There is undoubtedly a financial problem in the electricity sector. Power has a cost. Distribution companies require revenue, and transmission and distribution losses have historically presented a serious challenge. But the solution cannot perpetually be to transfer the consequences of inefficiency onto honest consumers. The first responsibility of government should be to reduce losses, improve billing and collection, prevent electricity theft, modernise infrastructure and improve the efficiency of distribution companies. A family that pays its electricity bill regularly should not become the easiest source for balancing the books. Before asking consumers to pay more, the government must demonstrate what measurable reduction it has achieved in distribution losses and what administrative reforms it has undertaken to bring down costs. Efficiency must come before additional burden. The government's defence does not answer the political question Chief Minister Omar Abdullah has defended the increase by arguing that the government never promised that electricity tariffs would remain static and that power continues to be substantially subsidised. That may constitute an administrative defence. It does not answer the political question. The issue is not whether electricity continues to receive subsidy. The issue is whether the government is moving towards the relief that was promised to the electorate or away from it. The people were promised 200 units of free electricity. They are entitled to ask when that promise will translate into meaningful relief in their monthly household budgets. A government cannot seek political credit for promises and subsequently seek refuge behind regulatory calculations when people demand their implementation. BJP must stand with the consumer The Bharatiya Janata Party should unequivocally stand with the ordinary electricity consumer of Jammu & Kashmir. This is not an issue concerning Jammu or Kashmir alone. A shopkeeper in Jammu, a middle-class employee in Kathua, a farmer in the countryside, a pensioner in Srinagar and a family facing the freezing winter in north or south Kashmir all ultimately confront the same question: How much more can the household budget absorb? The BJP should demand that the Omar Abdullah government reconsider the tariff increase, particularly its impact upon domestic consumers, and immediately place before the people a transparent roadmap for fulfilling its electricity-related electoral commitments. Special consideration should also be given to the extraordinary electricity requirements of Kashmir during the winter months. If necessary, the government should explore a targeted winter electricity relief mechanism for vulnerable and middle-income domestic consumers in the Valley rather than allowing climatic necessity to translate into financial punishment. Promises carry a moral obligation Democracy does not end when votes are counted. An electoral promise creates a political and moral obligation. Governments must either implement their promises or candidly explain why they cannot do so. What they cannot reasonably do is promise relief while seeking votes and subsequently impose additional burdens after coming to power. The people of Jammu & Kashmir have endured decades of difficulties. They deserve governance that reduces their burdens rather than adding to them. The BJP must therefore raise its voice firmly, both inside and outside the Legislature, and demand: Withdraw or substantially reconsider the burden of the power tariff hike on domestic consumers. Protect Kashmir's households during the harsh winter. Reduce distribution losses before passing costs to consumers. And, above all, honour the commitments made to the people. Electricity in Jammu & Kashmir—particularly during a Kashmir winter—is not merely another commodity. For many families, it is warmth. It is security. It is a basic necessity of life. And a government elected on promises of relief should remember that before making that necessity more expensive. Author is an advocate and Chief Spokesperson of BJP in J&K

stories.headline: Mirwaiz urges J&K political parties to strive for restoration of statehood, condemns threat to Kashmiri Pandits
stories.title: Mirwaiz urges J&K political parties to strive for restoration of statehood, condemns threat to Kashmiri Pandits
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 29: Kashmir chief cleric Mirwaiz Umar Farooq on Saturday asserted that political parties from Jammu and Kashmir should make efforts for restoration of statehood and Article 370, saying it is their moral responsibility to raise their voice for the rights of people. “Our rights were snatched away by force. Our statehood was abolished, we were made a Union territory. The government should uphold the promises made to people prior to the elections,” Farooq told reporters here. The preacher also termed alleged threats to Kashmiri Pandits residing in the Valley “deeply unfortunate”. “We have consistently reiterated that Kashmiri Pandits are an integral part of our society, history, culture, and our future. They are not outsiders, they belong here. We have always advocated for their return and will continue our efforts, as should the government,” he asserted. Lashing out at the NC-led government, the Mirwaiz accused it of losing sight of its priorities. They have been unable to instill confidence in people regarding their “snatched” rights, the splitting of Jammu and Kashmir, and the “complete disregard” for constitutional commitments, he added. He said the Centre had essentially revoked all the promises made to Jammu and Kashmir since 1947. “They revoked all constitutional guarantees. So, it is the moral responsibility of mainstream political parties to stand up for these issues. They must raise their voice for restoration of rights of the people of Jammu and Kashmir and present a unified voice in this regard,” he added. On Srinagar MP Ruhullah Mehdi’s decision to quit the Lok Sabha and the National Conference (NC), the Mirwaiz hailed the parliamentarian as a staunch voice committed to raising people’s issues, and urged all organisations and parties of Jammu and Kashmir to follow suit. “They must stand by these constitutional guarantees, the commitments they made to people, their manifesto, and their election plank,” he said. He also criticised the government over hike in electricity tariff. “The government must recognise that Jammu and Kashmir’s economy is already going through a very fragile phase. Common, low-income citizens are in no position to endure escalating power tariffs. The administration should have deferred this increase,” he said. The Mirwaiz expressed solidarity with the victims of the Nepal tragedy and their families, asserting that the flash flood disaster should serve as a warning for Jammu and Kashmir. “We also reside in this Himalayan region. Over the past couple of years, we have seen changing weather patterns and climatic shifts driven by global warming. God has blessed Kashmir with immense natural beauty. Protecting this is our foremost responsibility,” he said. He said while people want development, tourism and infrastructure, “it cannot come at the cost of our ecology and environment”. opening: Srinagar, Aug 29: Kashmir chief cleric Mirwaiz Umar Farooq on Saturday asserted that political parties from Jammu and Kashmir should make efforts for restoration of statehood and Article 370, saying it is their moral responsibility to raise their voice for the rights of people.
“Our rights were snatched away by force.
body: Our statehood was abolished, we were made a Union territory.
The government should uphold the promises made to people prior to the elections,” Farooq told reporters here.
The preacher also termed alleged threats to Kashmiri Pandits residing in the Valley “deeply unfortunate”.
“We have consistently reiterated that Kashmiri Pandits are an integral part of our society, history, culture, and our future.
They are not outsiders, they belong here.
We have always advocated for their return and will continue our efforts, as should the government,” he asserted.
Lashing out at the NC-led government, the Mirwaiz accused it of losing sight of its priorities.
They have been unable to instill confidence in people regarding their “snatched” rights, the splitting of Jammu and Kashmir, and the “complete disregard” for constitutional commitments, he added.
He said the Centre had essentially revoked all the promises made to Jammu and Kashmir since 1947.
“They revoked all constitutional guarantees.
So, it is the moral responsibility of mainstream political parties to stand up for these issues.
They must raise their voice for restoration of rights of the people of Jammu and Kashmir and present a unified voice in this regard,” he added.

On Srinagar MP Ruhullah Mehdi’s decision to quit the Lok Sabha and the National Conference (NC), the Mirwaiz hailed the parliamentarian as a staunch voice committed to raising people’s issues, and urged all organisations and parties of Jammu and Kashmir to follow suit.
“They must stand by these constitutional guarantees, the commitments they made to people, their manifesto, and their election plank,” he said.
He also criticised the government over hike in electricity tariff.
“The government must recognise that Jammu and Kashmir’s economy is already going through a very fragile phase.
Common, low-income citizens are in no position to endure escalating power tariffs.
The administration should have deferred this increase,” he said.
The Mirwaiz expressed solidarity with the victims of the Nepal tragedy and their families, asserting that the flash flood disaster should serve as a warning for Jammu and Kashmir.
“We also reside in this Himalayan region.
Over the past couple of years, we have seen changing weather patterns and climatic shifts driven by global warming.
God has blessed Kashmir with immense natural beauty.
Protecting this is our foremost responsibility,” he said.
He said while people want development, tourism and infrastructure, “it cannot come at the cost of our ecology and environment”.
Farooq said human interference with the ecosystem is largely responsible for weather vagaries and natural disasters.
“While we will hold the administration accountable, we must also introspect.
“Unplanned and unregulated construction continues unchecked across tourist destinations and fragile hilly terrains like Pahalgam.
If this persists, we are heading toward an ecological disaster.
Authorities and policy experts must formulate a well-structured roadmap to safeguard this Himalayan belt,” he said.

article_sentences: Suspicion grew after a Delhi-based entrepreneur was reportedly offered a ₹500-crore subcontract for solar projects.
A massive investment scam allegedly built around a fake US defence contract is unravelling following the arrest of a Kerala businessman by the Delhi.
Police.
Venkitta Venkittu, a native of Kollam and chairman of VPVV Techno Construction Private Limited, was detained in Hyderabad in connection with the case.
Investigators allege that the company lured investors across six Indian states by claiming that it had secured a lucrative contract to manufacture military weapons for the US Department of Defence.
The alleged fraud was initially estimated at around ₹700 crore.
However, investigators now fear that the amount involved could exceed ₹1,000 crore.
According to the investigation, the company allegedly made a series of claims to convince potential investors.
The suspect reportedly claimed to have 34 years of experience in the industry.
He is also alleged to have claimed that he played a key role in India’s Rafale fighter jet deal.
Official records, however, showed that the company’s assets were valued at less than ₹10 lakh.
When he sought further details about the offer, the company allegedly failed to provide them.
